content: Cross-dominance, also referred to as mixed-handedness, is a phenomenon in motor skills where an individual prefers one hand for certain tasks and the other hand for different tasks. This does not necessarily mean the person is ambidextrous, which refers to being equally skilled with both hands. For example, a person might write with their left hand but use their right hand to grab objects. Cross-dominance can also extend to mixed laterality, where a person shows preference for using eyes, ears, feet, or hands on opposite sides of the body. This condition can present challenges in activities requiring precise aim, such as shooting. The term ambidextrous originates from the Latin roots ambi, meaning both, and dexter, meaning right or favorable. Thus, ambidextrous literally translates to right on both sides. While true ambidexterity is rare at birth, it can be developed through practice. The process involves focusing on minor tasks and performing them daily with the non-dominant hand. Although initially difficult, tasks like brushing teeth, opening doors, and eating become easier with consistent effort. More complex skills, such as writing or throwing with both hands, require greater patience and practice but are achievable. In modern times, individuals who are considered ambidextrous are often those who were originally left-handed but adapted to using their right hand, either intentionally or due to societal pressures during childhood. For instance, schools often emphasize right-handed habits. Additionally, many everyday tools and devices are designed ergonomically for right-handed users, leaving left-handed individuals with no choice but to use their non-dominant hand. A common example is a can opener. Consequently, left-handed individuals are more likely to develop motor skills in their non-dominant hand compared to right-handed individuals, who are not typically exposed to left-hand-favoring devices. Ambidexterity is often encouraged in activities that demand high levels of skill in both hands, such as juggling, swimming, playing percussion or keyboard instruments, word processing, performing surgery, and engaging in combat. Popular Culture In baseball, three 19th-century pitchers are known to have thrown with both hands: Tony Mullane in 1882 and 1893, Elton Chamberlain in 1888, and Larry Corcoran in 1884. In the modern era, Greg A. Harris is the only major league pitcher to have pitched with both his left and right arms. A natural right-hander, by 1986, Harris had developed enough skill with his left hand to feel confident pitching with either hand during a game. However, he was not permitted to pitch left-handed in a regular-season game until September 28, 1995, during the penultimate game of his career. Playing for the Montreal Expos against the Cincinnati Reds, Harris retired Reggie Sanders pitching right-handed, then switched to his left hand to face two left-handed batters, Hal Morris and Ed Taubensee. He walked Morris but got Taubensee to ground out. Harris then returned to his right hand to retire Bret Boone and end the inning. In NCAA Division I baseball, Pat Venditte of the Creighton Bluejays regularly pitches with both arms. In snooker, Ronnie O'Sullivan is unique among top professionals for his ability to play at a world-class level with his left hand. While he lacks power in his left arm, his ability to switch hands allows him to take shots that would otherwise require awkward cueing. When he first demonstrated this skill during the 1996 World Championship against Alain Robidoux, the Canadian accused him of disrespect. O'Sullivan responded by stating that he played better with his left hand than Robidoux could with his right. O'Sullivan was summoned to a disciplinary hearing following Robidoux's formal complaint, where he had to prove his proficiency with his left hand. He played three frames of snooker against former world championship runner-up Rex Williams, winning all three. The charge of bringing the game into disrepute was subsequently dropped. In golf, Mac O'Grady was a touring professional who played right-handed but could play scratch golf (no handicap) left-handed. He lobbied the USGA for years to be certified as an amateur left-handed player and a professional right-handed player, but his efforts were unsuccessful. In ice hockey, Gordie Howe used a hockey stick with an uncurved blade, allowing him to play effectively with either hand. In music, Chris Martin, the lead singer, pianist, and occasional rhythm guitarist of the band Coldplay, writes with his left hand, plays the guitar in the orthodox (right-handed) manner, and draws with his right hand. Etymology In English, the term ambidexter was originally used in a legal context to describe jurors who accepted bribes from both parties in a case. Jurors found guilty of such bribery were required to forfeit decies tantum, an amount ten times greater than what they had received in bribes.
